title: Uber Is Building Its First Data Centre in India — and It Picked Adani to Do It
excerpt: The $500 million hyperscale facility marks a bet on India's digital infrastructure boom. For the diaspora tech workforce that built Uber's algorithms, the move brings the code closer to home.
body:
Uber and the Adani Group have confirmed they are building a $500 million hyperscale data centre in India — Uber's first on Indian soil — in a deal that positions the country as a critical node in the ride-hailing giant's global technology stack.

The announcement came during a five-day visit by Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, who met Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, G20 Sherpa Amitabh Kant, and senior officials at the CII Annual Business Summit in Delhi. The data centre, to be developed through Adani's data infrastructure arm AdaniConneX, is expected to be operational by the end of 2026.

The move signals a fundamental shift in how global technology companies view India — no longer just as a market for consumers or a source of engineering talent, but as a place to house the physical infrastructure that runs their most critical operations.

## Why India, Why Now

Uber's decision to locate a data centre in India is driven by three converging forces.

The first is regulatory. India's data localisation policies, which have tightened steadily since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023, increasingly require companies to store and process Indian user data within national borders. For Uber, which operates in over 100 Indian cities and has quadrupled its platform earner base in the country since 2022, compliance is not optional — it is the cost of staying in the market.

The second is economic. India's data centre market is projected to grow from $10.5 billion in 2025 to $45 billion by 2033, according to industry estimates. Uber is not entering a niche — it is joining a stampede. Google recently announced a $15 billion AI hub in Visakhapatnam in partnership with Adani and Bharti Airtel. Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle have all expanded their Indian data centre footprints in 2026.

The third is strategic. Uber increasingly views India not just as a local market but as a global innovation hub. The company's engineering teams in Bengaluru and Hyderabad already work on core platform features used worldwide. Having a local data centre accelerates testing, deployment, and the AI workloads that Khosrowshahi has identified as central to Uber's future — from route optimisation to dynamic pricing to autonomous vehicle integration.

## The Adani Factor

The choice of Adani as the infrastructure partner carries its own significance. AdaniConneX, a joint venture between the Adani Group and EdgeConneX, has emerged as one of India's fastest-growing data centre operators. The company has committed over $100 billion to AI-ready data infrastructure by 2035 — a number that would have seemed fantastical a few years ago but now sits within the range of what hyperscale computing demands.

For the Adani Group, the Uber partnership reinforces its pivot from ports, power, and airports into the digital economy. Gautam Adani has positioned data centres as the next great infrastructure play — and he is not wrong. The energy, land, cooling, and connectivity requirements of modern data centres map neatly onto the capabilities that the Adani conglomerate already possesses.

Critics will note that partnering with Adani carries reputational risk, particularly in Western markets. The group's recent $18 million SEC settlement over its green bond case (with both sides seeking consent judgments) remains fresh in memory. But for Uber, the calculation is straightforward: Adani builds infrastructure at a scale and speed that few Indian companies can match.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

The Uber-Adani data centre is another brick in the edifice of what some analysts call 'India's digital sovereignty moment' — the point at which the country's technology infrastructure becomes self-sufficient enough to compete with, rather than depend on, Western cloud regions.

For the tens of thousands of Indian-origin engineers who work at Uber globally — in San Francisco, Amsterdam, and Bengaluru — the data centre represents a tangible link between the code they write and the country many of them come from. When Khosrowshahi told the CII audience that India had 'evolved beyond a market into a technology partner,' he was describing a reality that diaspora tech workers have been advocating for years.

The broader signal is for NRI professionals weighing return-to-India decisions. The argument that India lacks the infrastructure to support cutting-edge technology work grows weaker with each billion-dollar data centre announcement. When Uber, Google, and Microsoft are all building hyperscale facilities on Indian soil, the infrastructure gap that once made Silicon Valley irreplaceable is narrowing.

## The Competition

Uber's Indian data centre also reflects defensive positioning. The company holds roughly 50 per cent of India's ride-hailing market but faces aggressive competition from Ola and the rapidly growing Rapido, which recently surpassed both Uber and Ola in monthly active users.

Local data infrastructure gives Uber lower latency, better performance, and potentially lower costs — advantages that matter in a market where margins are thin and user loyalty is fleeting. It also positions the company to offer localised services — from payments integration to government partnerships — that would be impossible to run efficiently from data centres in Singapore or Virginia.

Khosrowshahi's India visit was notably high-touch for a market that Uber once treated as a secondary priority. The meetings with Sitharaman and Kant, the CII keynote, and the Adani partnership announcement collectively signal that India has moved from Uber's emerging-markets playbook to its core strategic agenda.

The $500 million question is whether the investment will translate into market dominance — or whether Rapido and Ola will continue to eat Uber's lunch while it builds the kitchen.
